questions.q: Why does Kantorovich relax Monge's problem from transport maps to couplings $\pi\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)$?
choices: A transport map cannot split the mass sitting at a single point, so a Monge map may fail to exist; couplings allow a source point's mass to be spread over several targets
Couplings are cheaper to transport than maps for the same configuration
Maps are not measurable in general, whereas couplings always are
The Monge cost $\int c(x,T(x))\,d\mu$ is non-linear, while the coupling cost is quadratic
questions.explain: A map $T$ sends all the mass at $x$ to the single point $T(x)$. If $\mu=\delta_0$ and $\nu=\tfrac12\delta_{-1}+\tfrac12\delta_{1}$, no map can push $\mu$ to $\nu$ — the atom must split. The Kantorovich coupling $\pi$ records how much mass goes from $x$ to $y$, so splitting is allowed and the problem (a linear program) always has a minimizer.

questions.q: A coupling $\pi$ on $X\times Y$ belongs to $\Pi(\mu,\nu)$ exactly when:
choices: its two marginals are $\mu$ and $\nu$: $\pi(A\times Y)=\mu(A)$ and $\pi(X\times B)=\nu(B)$
it is supported on the diagonal $\{x=y\}$
it minimizes $\int c\,d\pi$ among all probability measures on $X\times Y$
questions.explain:
$\Pi(\mu,
u)$ is the set of all probability measures on $X	imes Y$ with first marginal $\mu$ and second marginal $
u$ — the transportation polytope. The product measure $\mu\otimes
u$ is always one such coupling (independent transport), so $\Pi$ is never empty; optimality is a separate condition.

questions.q: Two unit masses sit at sources $s_1,s_2$; two unit sinks $t_1,t_2$ must each receive one unit. The cost matrix is $c=\begin{pmatrix}1&3\\4&2\end{pmatrix}$ (entry $c_{ij}$ = cost to move $s_i\to t_j$). What is the minimum total transport cost?
questions.explain: With unit masses the optimum is a permutation (Birkhoff: the assignment polytope's vertices are permutation matrices). Compare the identity assignment $c_{11}+c_{22}=1+2=3$ against the swap $c_{12}+c_{21}=3+4=7$. The minimum is $3$.

questions.q: At the optimum of the transport LP, the dual potentials satisfy $\varphi(x)+\psi(y)\le c(x,y)$ everywhere. What does complementary slackness say about where this is an equality?
choices: Equality holds exactly on the support of the optimal plan $\pi$
Equality holds on the diagonal $x=y$ only
Equality holds on a set of full $\mu\otimes\nu$ measure
questions.explain: Strong duality forces $\int(\varphi\oplus\psi)\,d\pi=\int c\,d\pi$ at the optimum. Since $\varphi(x)+\psi(y)\le c(x,y)$ pointwise and $\pi$ has the right marginals, the integrands can only agree where $\varphi(x)+\psi(y)=c(x,y)$. Hence $\pi$ is concentrated on that tight set — this is what locates the optimal transport geometrically.

questions.q: Kantorovich–Rubinstein duality writes $W_1(\mu,\nu)$ as a supremum over which class of test functions?
questions.explain: For the cost $c(x,y)=|x-y|$ the $c$-transform forces $\psi=-\varphi$ with $\varphi$ being $1$-Lipschitz, collapsing the two-potential dual to $W_1(\mu,\nu)=\sup_{\mathrm{Lip}(f)\le1}\int f\,d(\mu-\nu)$. This is why $W_1$ is also called the earth-mover / Kantorovich–Rubinstein distance and appears as the metric dual to Lipschitz functions.

questions.q: On the real line with cost $c(x,y)=|x-y|$, let $\mu=\delta_0$ and $\nu=\delta_3$. What is $W_1(\mu,\nu)$?
questions.explain: There is only one coupling of two Diracs, so $W_1=\int|x-y|\,d\pi=|0-3|=3$. Dually, the $1$-Lipschitz potential $f(x)=-x$ gives $\int f\,d\mu-\int f\,d\nu=0-(-3)=3$, attaining the bound.

questions.q: In one dimension, $W_2$ between two Gaussians is $W_2^2=|m_1-m_2|^2+(\sigma_1-\sigma_2)^2$. Compute $W_2\big(\mathcal{N}(0,1),\mathcal{N}(3,1)\big)$ (here the second argument is the variance, so $\sigma=1$ for both).
questions.explain: Means $0$ and $3$, equal standard deviations $\sigma_1=\sigma_2=1$. So $W_2^2=(3-0)^2+(1-1)^2=9$ and $W_2=3$. With equal shape, transport is a pure translation and $W_2$ equals the distance the mean moves.

questions.q: Same formula, now equal means but different spreads: compute $W_2\big(\mathcal{N}(0,1),\mathcal{N}(0,4)\big)$ (variances $1$ and $4$, so $\sigma_1=1,\sigma_2=2$).
questions.explain: $W_2^2=(0-0)^2+(1-2)^2=1$, so $W_2=1$. Even with matched means, $W_2$ sees the difference in spread — the optimal map stretches the standard normal by a factor of $2$ about the mean.

questions.q: Take $\mu=\delta_0$ and $\mu_\varepsilon=\delta_\varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon\to0$. How do total variation and $W_2$ behave?
choices: both tend to $0$ at the same linear rate
both stay equal to $1$ for all $\varepsilon$
questions.explain: Two distinct Diracs are mutually singular, so $\mathrm{TV}=1$ no matter how close they are — TV is blind to geometry. $W_2$ measures the actual displacement, $W_2(\delta_0,\delta_\varepsilon)=\varepsilon$, so it $\to0$. This is exactly why $W_p$ metrizes weak convergence and TV does not.

questions.q: For quadratic cost $\tfrac12|x-y|^2$ with $\mu$ absolutely continuous, Brenier's theorem says the optimal transport map has what special form?
choices: $T=\nabla\varphi$ for a convex potential $\varphi$, and this $T$ is unique $\mu$-a.e.
$T$ is the gradient of an arbitrary smooth function
questions.explain: Brenier: the $c$-concave Kantorovich potential $\psi$ makes $x\mapsto\tfrac12|x|^2-\psi(x)=\varphi(x)$ convex, and the optimal map is $T=\nabla\varphi$, unique $\mu$-a.e. So the relaxed Kantorovich problem collapses back to a genuine Monge map — but only because the cost is quadratic and $\mu$ has no atoms.

questions.q: In one dimension, the Brenier (quadratic-cost) optimal map from $\mu$ to $\nu$ is:
choices: any measurable bijection matching the supports
$T(x)=\mathbb{E}_\nu[Y]$, a constant map to the target mean
questions.explain:
Convexity of $\varphi$ in 1D means $T=\varphi'$ is non-decreasing. The unique non-decreasing map pushing $\mu$ to $
u$ is the quantile coupling $T=F_
u^{-1}\circ F_\mu$: it sends the $q$-quantile of $\mu$ to the $q$-quantile of $
u$. The decreasing rearrangement is in fact the worst (cost-maximizing) coupling.

questions.q: Let $\mu=\mathrm{Unif}[0,1]$ and $\nu=\mathrm{Unif}[0,3]$. The 1D Brenier map is $T=F_\nu^{-1}\circ F_\mu$. Evaluate $T(0.5)$.
questions.explain: $F_\mu(x)=x$ on $[0,1]$ and $F_\nu^{-1}(q)=3q$ on $[0,1]$, so $T(x)=3x$. Then $T(0.5)=1.5$ — the map stretches $[0,1]$ uniformly onto $[0,3]$, which is exactly the monotone increasing rearrangement.

questions.q: Which curve is the constant-speed geodesic between $\mu$ and $\nu$ in $(\mathcal{P}_2,W_2)$?
choices: displacement interpolation $\mu_t=((1-t)\,\mathrm{id}+t\,T)_\#\mu$, transporting mass along straight lines
linear interpolation $\mu_t=(1-t)\mu+t\nu$, fading one measure out and the other in
the geometric mean of the densities, $\mu_t\propto\rho_\mu^{1-t}\rho_\nu^{t}$
the heat-flow regularization of $\mu$ run for time $t$
questions.explain: McCann's displacement interpolation uses the Brenier map $T$ and moves each particle along the segment from $x$ to $T(x)$. The linear interpolation $(1-t)\mu+t\nu$ is the geodesic for the flat $L^2$/TV geometry, not $W_2$: it just dims one bump and brightens another instead of sliding mass across.

questions.q: For two point masses, the $W_2$ geodesic between $\delta_a$ and $\delta_b$ is:
choices: $\delta_{(1-t)a+tb}$ — a single atom travelling along the segment $[a,b]$
questions.explain: The only coupling of two Diracs sends $a\mapsto b$, so the displacement geodesic is $\delta_{(1-t)a+tb}$: the atom moves at constant speed along the line. The weighted version $(1-t)\delta_a+t\delta_b$ is the (non-geodesic in $W_2$) linear interpolation and has length-mismatched, non-constant Wasserstein speed.

questions.q: Displacement interpolation between $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ and $\mathcal{N}(4,1)$ stays Gaussian with linearly interpolated mean and standard deviation. What is the mean of $\mu_{t}$ at $t=\tfrac12$?
questions.explain: Means interpolate linearly: $m_t=(1-t)\cdot0+t\cdot4=4t$, so $m_{1/2}=2$. The standard deviation stays $1$ throughout (both endpoints have $\sigma=1$), so $\mu_{1/2}=\mathcal{N}(2,1)$ — a single bump that has slid halfway, not two half-height bumps.

ot-gradient-flows.title: Otto calculus and JKO gradient flows

questions.q: In Otto's picture, the heat equation $\partial_t\rho=\Delta\rho$ is the $W_2$ gradient flow of which functional?
questions.explain:
The general $W_2$ gradient flow of $F$ is $\partial_tho=
abla\!\cdot(ho\,
abla F'(ho))$. For $F(ho)=\intho\logho$ we have $F'(ho)=\logho+1$, so $ho
abla F'(ho)=ho\,
abla\logho=
ablaho$ and the flow is $\partial_tho=\Deltaho$. This is the Jordan–Kinderlehrer–Otto discovery: diffusion = steepest entropy descent in Wasserstein geometry.

questions.q: The JKO minimizing-movement scheme builds the flow by iterating which step (time-step $\tau$)?
questions.explain: JKO is the implicit Euler / minimizing-movement step but with the metric being $W_2$ instead of an $L^2$ norm: each step trades off proximity to $\mu_k$ (measured by $W_2^2/2\tau$) against decreasing the energy $F$. As $\tau\to0$ the piecewise-constant interpolation converges to the gradient flow $\partial_t\rho=\nabla\!\cdot(\rho\nabla F'(\rho))$.

With $F(ho)=\intho\logho+\int Vho$, the first variation is $F'(ho)=\logho+1+V$, so $ho
